title: Volatile Data
summary: Volatile data is state that exists only while a system is powered, running or connected: processor registers and cache contents, random access memory, running processes and their loaded modules, open network sockets and routing tables, logged-on sessions, mounted encrypted volumes, clipboard contents, and in-memory credentials or keys. Because it disappears on shutdown, reboot, logoff, container termination or network disconnection, it is both the most perishable and often the most probative evidence in an investigation. Memory is where fileless malware, injected code, decryption keys, command-and-control configuration and unencrypted artefacts frequently live, and where a rootkit's tampering may be visible even when the file system looks clean. Established practice follows an order of volatility, collecting the fastest-decaying sources first: processor and memory state, then network and process state, then temporary file systems, then disk, then archival media. Acquisition must be planned before the responder types a single command, because ordinary administrative actions such as listing directories, opening a file or running a built-in utility overwrite memory and alter timestamps. Captured data is hashed, documented and stored under chain of custody, and analysis must account for the fact that memory contents are a snapshot of a live and constantly changing system. In virtualised and cloud environments the practical techniques differ, relying on hypervisor snapshots, managed capture APIs and provider tooling, but the ordering logic and the documentation obligations do not change.
objectives: Classify data sources by volatility and apply the correct collection order at an incident scene.
Explain why memory, session and network state often carry evidence that the file system does not.
Plan a volatile data collection sequence that avoids overwriting evidence through routine administrative commands.
Capture memory, process, network and session state using validated tooling and hash the resulting output.
Adapt volatile collection techniques to virtual machines, containers and cloud instances.
Document volatile acquisitions so that they satisfy chain of custody and remain usable in later analysis.
Assess the investigative cost of a reboot, shutdown or logoff and communicate that cost to decision makers.

beginner.definition: Volatile data is information that only exists while a system is switched on and running. Examples include memory contents, running programs, open network connections, and logged-in sessions. As soon as the machine shuts down, reboots, or disconnects, this data is gone. That makes it the most fragile evidence in an investigation.
beginner.whyItMatters: Some of the best evidence never reaches the disk. Fileless attacks, encryption keys, and active connections live only in memory and system state. If your first action is a restart, that evidence disappears before you can look at it. The order in which you collect data decides what you can still prove later.
howItWorks: Start with the fastest to disappear: memory contents and the running state of the system.
Next capture the active network connections and the list of running programs.
Then record who is logged in and which encrypted drives are currently unlocked.
Only after that move to slower material, such as temporary files and then the disk.
Avoid ordinary commands that change the system, because they can overwrite evidence.
Save each capture with a hash, a time, and a note about who collected it.
beginner.example: Think of snow on a warm morning. If you want to study the shape of the flakes, you must look before the sun climbs higher. Once the snow melts, the pattern is gone and no tool brings it back. Volatile data is that snow. Collect it first, and write down what you saw.
takeaways: Volatile data vanishes on a shutdown, a reboot, a logoff, or a disconnect.
Collect in order of fragility: memory first, then connections, then disk.
Everyday commands change the system, so plan your collection before you type.
